newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala hopes to increase exports to Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala hopes to increase exports to Mexico.

text.p: Guatemala's private sector could quadruple exports to Mexico under a free trade treaty that will enter its fourth round of negotiations on Tuesday in Mexico City, a business representative said.

"Mexico being such a big country that imports everything, why can't we increase our exports from 5-6 percent (of yearly total) to 20 percent," Enrique Lacs, coordinator of a business group that advises the Guatemalan government's free trade negotiating team, told Reuters in a recent interview.
Central America's so-called Northern Triangle -- Guatemala, El Salvador and Honduras -- began negotiating a free trade agreement with Mexico last September.

The Northern Triangle previously established its negotiating position as a block and the three countries have already begun to reduce and standardize tariffs. This week's round of talks with Mexico lasts through Friday and Lacs said the treaty could be completed in early 1998.
Lacs said Guatemalan producers of traditional agricultural exports such as coffee, bananas and sugar have their fears about free trade, but hope they will export to Mexico.
"Mexico imports a huge amount of agricultural products ...but the dilemma of this entire negotiation is that our access to Mexico has been very complicated," Lacs said.
Guatemala's trade deficit with Mexico was approximately $210 million last year said Lacs.
Under free trade, Guatemala could sell $20 million worth of sugar to Mexico every year and enter southern Mexican markets with beer, candy, textiles, plastics and beef.

Lacs said rules of origin have been among the most sensitive aspects of the negotiations so far. Negotiators have agreed that rules of origin will use a flexible method based on the principal raw material in any given product, he said.

Negotiating sanitary regulations was easy because they are based on international norms, Lacs said, adding that the treaty would have to take into account the technical, geographic and climatological realities of Central America.
"We have a lot of micro-climates and isolated areas so it is hard to declare a large area free of pests," Lacs said.
Lacs said the negotiators were also seeking a formula to take into account huge subsidies by the Mexican government to agricultural and manufacturing businesses.

Nicaragua has suspended its own free trade negotiations with Mexico and could become a member of the Northern Triangle agreement after it is negotiated, Lacs said. Costa Rica already has its own free trade pact with Mexico.
